solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Hates working for someone who might wield the axe

definitions.text: someone who might wield the axe

parts.note: to abhor something is to hate it
a machine that is working is switched on

explanation.surface: Someone who hates their job ends up working for a boss who might fire them, or worse.
explanation.walkthrough: ABHORSON is the executioner in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure, who takes on Pompey as his assistant.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's headsman in Measure for Measure is the character whose trade is beheading prisoners.

clue.text: Motion responsible for a blow to the head

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the first name of the poet Motion, Poet Laureate from 1999 to 2009

definitions.text: responsible for a blow to the head
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the foolish knight in Twelfth Night who starts the brawl with Sebastian and comes off worst

explanation.walkthrough: Motion looks like a proposal or a movement, but it is the surname of Andrew Motion; Sir ANDREW Aguecheek trades blows with Sebastian in Twelfth Night.
explanation.definitionFit: Both meanings are people named Andrew: the modern Poet Laureate and Shakespeare's knight caught up in a fight in Illyria.

clue.text: Permitted to support an actor who reveals the plot of the Mousetrap

definitions.text: who reveals the plot of the Mousetrap

indicators.note: in a down entry, the piece that supports another sits underneath it, so it comes second

parts.note: a ham is an actor who overacts
let means allowed or permitted

explanation.surface: An actor is allowed to blurt out the twist of Agatha Christie's long-running whodunnit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mousetrap suggests Christie's play, but here it is the play within Shakespeare's play, staged by HAMLET to expose Claudius's murder plot.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish prince stages a play he calls The Mousetrap to show up his uncle's crime before the court.

clue.text: "The dagger was 'good for killing fish,' he said —; … fish upon two legs." (In the South Seas, R.L. Stevenson)

definitions.text: "The dagger was 'good for killing fish,' he said —; … fish upon two legs." (In the South Seas, R.L. Stevenson)

parts.words: "The dagger was 'good for killing fish,' he said —; … fish upon two legs." (In the South Seas, R.L. Stevenson)
parts.note: the surface: a quotation with a word missing after 'he said', which looks like a puzzle about the dagger or the fish; the setter's reading: the gap is an adverb from Stevenson's travel book, describing a speaker hinting slyly that the 'fish upon two legs' were people

explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-gap clue: the missing word follows 'he said' in Stevenson's text, ROGUISHLY, since the man jokes that his dagger was really for killing men.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb describes the mischievous, sly way the islander makes his grim joke about two-legged fish.

clue.text: Plant two owls and a hen here

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a wild clematis whose fluffy seed heads look like grey whiskers

definitions.text: two owls and a hen here
definitions.meaning: second meaning: in an Edward Lear limerick, two owls and a hen, four larks and a wren all nest in a certain old fellow's whiskers

explanation.walkthrough: Lear's first limerick runs: There was an Old Man with a beard, who said, 'It is just as I feared! Two Owls and a Hen, four Larks and a Wren, have all built their nests in my beard!'
explanation.definitionFit: Old man's beard is a common name for wild clematis, and in Lear's nonsense verse it is literally where the birds nest.

clue.text: One of the Ladies' Day girls recalled longing to embrace men

definitions.text: One of the Ladies' Day girls

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in the arms, so the reversed word wraps around the next piece
something recalled is called back, so the word for longing is read from its end

parts.note: a need is a longing or want
OR, other ranks, is the usual crossword abbreviation for soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: A woman at the races remembers wanting to put her arms round some men.
explanation.walkthrough: Ladies' Day is a comedy by Amanda Whittington about four fish-factory workers on a day out at Royal Ascot; DOREEN is a name of that period.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a woman's name, matching the setter's description of a character from the play about the day at the races.

clue.text: Only seconds from losing Ezra Pound in Leucothea's sea air

indicators.note: only seconds means nothing but the second letter of each word that follows is kept

parts.note: the second letters of these five words, read in order

explanation.surface: A poet is momentarily lost overboard in the sea of Leucothea, the sea goddess who rescues Odysseus and appears in Pound's Cantos.
explanation.walkthrough: Ezra Pound and Leucothea are there for the literary surface; only the second letter of each of the five words matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ozone is the popular name for the bracing smell of fresh air at the seaside.

clue.text: Member states made no changes to an ancient port

indicators.note: the word changes here is a verb applied to the words before it, so their letters are altered into a new order

parts.note: the European Union is a body made up of member states
these six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Member states refuse to make any changes in their treatment of an old harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: Made no changes reads like a refusal to alter anything; really changes is the anagram signal working on the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Eudaemon Arabia was the classical name for the Red Sea harbour now known as Aden.

clue.text: Those magnificent and angry men make this?

definitions.meaning: the surface: a group of grand and furious men, perhaps from the film about flying machines
the setter's reading: add up the Magnificent Seven and the Twelve Angry Men from two famous film titles

explanation.walkthrough: Those magnificent men recalls the flying-machine film, but the sum needs The Magnificent Seven plus Twelve Angry Men: seven and twelve make NINETEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: The total of the two numbers in the film titles is the number given by the answer.

clue.text: Dido's gem replaced 20 and more of similar origins

indicators.note: replaced means put back in a different place, so the letters are set down in a new order

parts.note: every letter of these words, with the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Queen Dido's jewel was swapped for another, by Aeneas and others born like him.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 is 20-down, AENEAS, Dido's lover and son of the goddess Venus by a mortal father; others with one divine parent are DEMIGODS.
explanation.definitionFit: Beings born of one god and one mortal, like Aeneas, are half-divine heroes of mixed parentage.

clue.text: Tory party name for a political novelist

parts.note: Con is the abbreviation for Conservative, the party of the Tories
a do is a party or celebration
N is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A Conservative party chooses a name for a novelist who writes about politics.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard CONDON wrote The Manchurian Candidate, a thriller about political assassination and brainwashing.
explanation.definitionFit: The American author of The Manchurian Candidate wrote satirical thrillers about politics and power.

clue.text: One affords tight control of stock by doing reordering

indicators.note: reordering means putting into a different sequence, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: every letter of these three words

explanation.surface: A manager keeps a tight grip on the stock by doing the reordering personally.
explanation.walkthrough: Tight control suggests strict management of a shop's stock, but it is a garment that holds the figure in.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-piece close-fitting garment covering the torso and legs gives firm shaping to the figure.

clue.text: Resin used in ink made by the Spanish music publishers in the past

parts.note: el is the Spanish masculine form of the
EMI was a major British record company and music publisher, now absorbed into other groups

explanation.surface: A resin used in printing ink was produced by a Spanish music publisher of old.
explanation.definitionFit: Elemi is a fragrant tropical tree gum used in varnishes, printing inks and perfumes.

clue.text: A character represented to the audience what Briony was looking for

parts.note: taken as written
the tone of something is its character or general quality

indicators.note: something presented to an audience is heard, so the last piece counts by its sound

parts.note: what a sign represents is what it meant; that word heard gives a common word ending

explanation.surface: An actor performs a character for an audience, perhaps in a stage version of a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Briony Tallis spends Ian McEwan's novel ATONEMENT trying to make amends for a false accusation she made as a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Briony seeks to make amends for her crime, and making amends for a wrong is the meaning of the novel's title.

clue.text: Cabinet Minister broke up with this short Bond girl

definitions.text: Cabinet Minister broke up with this

parts.note: a short is a small measure of spirits, as opposed to a long drink
Pussy Galore is the Bond girl in Goldfinger

explanation.surface: A Cabinet Minister ends an affair with a petite woman from a James Bond film.
explanation.walkthrough: In Compton Mackenzie's novel the SS Cabinet Minister runs aground off a Hebridean island with a cargo of whisky; Cabinet Minister is a ship, not a politician.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel and its film are named for the abundance of spirits the islanders salvage from the wrecked cargo ship.

clue.text: At first Atticus follows a system of laws; and then runs into his sister!

indicators.note: follows says the letter from Atticus comes after everything else in the clue's wordplay

parts.note: taken as written
lex is Latin for law, used for a body of law
taken as written
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letter of the name Atticus is used

parts.note: the opening letter of this name

explanation.surface: Atticus Finch keeps to the law, then bumps into his sister.
explanation.walkthrough: In To Kill a Mockingbird, Atticus Finch's sister is Aunt ALEXANDRA, who moves in to look after Scout.
explanation.definitionFit: Harper Lee gives Atticus a strict, proper sibling who comes to stay with his family in Maycomb.

clue.text: Ion maybe overheard what Drake does to a Nightingale?

indicators.note: overheard means caught by ear, so the phrase that follows is to be said out loud

parts.words: what Drake does to a Nightingale
parts.note: Drake is a rapper, and Keats wrote an ode to a nightingale

explanation.surface: Someone overhears a duck making noises at a songbird.
explanation.walkthrough: Drake looks like a male duck, but it is the Canadian rapper; Ion is the reciter of Homer in Plato's dialogue Ion, a RHAPSODE.
explanation.definitionFit: Plato's Ion is a professional reciter of epic poetry, an example of the ancient Greek performers of Homer.

clue.text: He wrote The Red Bow as Red Sun originally

indicators.note: originally hints that the name was these letters in another order before it was rearranged; a loose signal

parts.note: every letter of these three words

explanation.surface: An author first wrote his story The Red Bow under the title Red Sun.
explanation.walkthrough: George SAUNDERS wrote the short story The Red Bow, collected in In Persuasion Nation.
explanation.definitionFit: The American short-story writer and Booker winner is the author of that tale about a town's dog cull.

clue.text: Hard work made of writing, with a pig eating the manuscript

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the idiom for making a task seem much harder than it is

definitions.text: writing, with a pig eating the manuscript
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a Wodehouse Blandings novel in which feeding Galahad's scandalous memoirs to the Empress of Blandings is proposed

explanation.walkthrough: To make heavy weather of something is to struggle needlessly with it; Heavy Weather is also P.G. Wodehouse's Blandings novel about the fate of Galahad's memoirs.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes making a laborious job of something, and the Wodehouse novel title fits the writing described.

clue.text: This festival has one rule I'd counter

indicators.note: counter means running in the opposite direction, so the joined pieces are read backwards

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
a law is a rule
the apostrophe is dropped

explanation.surface: A festival has a rule that someone says they would oppose.
explanation.walkthrough: Counter looks like the verb oppose; it signals turning the whole string round.
explanation.definitionFit: Diwali is the Hindu, Sikh and Jain festival of lights held each autumn.

clue.text: Every other one deserted a teen because he married Creusa

indicators.note: every other one deserted means alternate letters are dropped, leaving the first, third, fifth and so on

parts.note: starting from the first letter, keep every second one

explanation.surface: Someone abandoned a teenager because he had married another woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Deserted hints at the hero who deserted Dido; here it removes letters. Creusa was the first wife of AENEAS, lost in the fall of Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Aeneid, the Trojan hero's first wife Creusa, daughter of Priam, dies as they flee burning Troy.

clue.text: In alarm about 'Turning … gyre', Auden wrote one for Yeats

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for alarm goes round the mixed letters

parts.note: panic is sudden alarm

indicators.note: turning means twisting about, so the letters of the quoted word are mixed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Auden, alarmed by Yeats's line 'Turning and turning in the widening gyre', wrote him a tribute.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is the opening of Yeats's The Second Coming; Auden's In Memory of W.B. Yeats is a PANEGYRIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A panegyric is a public speech or poem of praise, which Auden's elegy on Yeats's death is.

clue.text: Starting for Eldorado with a light heart

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the opening word of Poe's poem Eldorado, '... bedight, a gallant knight'
second meaning: cheerfully, in a happy carefree way

explanation.surface: Someone sets off to find the city of gold in a cheerful mood.
explanation.walkthrough: Starting for Eldorado looks like setting off on a quest, but it means the first word of Edgar Allan Poe's poem.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means cheerfully or merrily, in a light-hearted manner, as Poe's knight rides out.

clue.text: She encountered a snap-dragon-fly in an article on insects

indicators.note: in an across entry, one piece on another comes before it, so the article leads

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
lice are small parasitic insects

explanation.surface: A girl met a strange dragonfly in a magazine article about insects.
explanation.walkthrough: In Through the Looking-Glass the Gnat tells ALICE about the Snap-dragon-fly, whose body is plum-pudding and whose head is a raisin burning in brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's heroine hears about the looking-glass insects, including this one, on her journey.

clue.text: He killed Lensky using a single shot

parts.note: a single thing is one
a shot is a measure of spirit, here a familiar one

explanation.surface: A duellist kills his friend with just one shot.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene ONEGIN, in Pushkin's verse novel and Tchaikovsky's opera, kills his friend Lensky in a duel; the shot is a drink, not a bullet.
explanation.definitionFit: Pushkin's hero shoots the young poet Lensky dead in a duel fought over Olga.

clue.text: Margaret Drabble's summer place, with many bars

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Drabble's first novel is titled with a summer version of this object

definitions.note: this describes the thing rather than naming it; read it as 'a place with many bars'
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an enclosure for a pet with lots of thin metal rods

explanation.surface: A novelist's holiday home has plenty of pubs nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Drabble's first novel is A Summer BIRD-CAGE; the bars are wires, not pubs.
explanation.definitionFit: A cage for birds is made of many closely spaced wires, and it supplies the second half of Drabble's title.

clue.text: Trials taken on by Hercules, say: stoically

indicators.note: taken on by means held within, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run consecutively across the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Hercules endures his labours with stoic patience.
explanation.walkthrough: Trials suggests the labours of Hercules; ESSAYS is an old sense of trials or attempts.
explanation.definitionFit: An essay originally meant an attempt or try, from the French essayer, to try.

clue.text: Fashion suiting a friend of Little Chandler

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so the letters are worked into a new form

parts.note: every letter of these two words

explanation.surface: A smart suit for a friend of a man called Little Chandler.
explanation.walkthrough: Fashion looks like a noun about clothes; it is a verb. In Joyce's story A Little Cloud, Little Chandler envies his old friend IGNATIUS Gallaher.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignatius Gallaher is the successful journalist whom Little Chandler meets for a drink in Joyce's Dubliners story.
